meta.title: Who really said "We go to openings of envelopes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Warhol said it — quoted in The Christian Science Monitor, 18 Aug 1977. The envelope joke itself was Jack O’Brian’s 1974 barb at Sylvia Miles.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We go to openings of envelopes'?
meta.ogDescription: Warhol really said it in 1977 — but the ‘opening of an envelope’ joke started as a 1974 barb at actress Sylvia Miles.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1928–1987 · American pop artist, filmmaker & co-founder of Interview magazine
answer.sourceLine: Warhol really did say this, in the first person: “We go to openings of envelopes, openings of books — which are better — and closings of doors,” quoted in Melvin Maddocks’s column “Cold showers and parties,” The Christian Science Monitor, 18 August 1977. What he did not do is invent the joke — the earliest version Quote Investigator can find ↗ is Broadway columnist Jack O’Brian’s barb at actress Sylvia Miles, printed in January 1974.

source.heading: The column that records it

docMeta.dd: The Christian Science Monitor (Boston), 18 August 1977, p. 26, col. 3
Jack O’Brian, “The Voice of Broadway,” The Jersey Journal, 23 January 1974

source.excerpt: I never go out alone. I am always surrounded by my entourage at any party. We go to openings of envelopes, openings of books — which are better — and closings of doors. That is to say, we go out a lot. But I still don’t understand or believe in parties.
trail: 23 January 1974 — the earliest version Quote Investigator locates ↗ runs in Jack O’Brian’s Broadway column in The Jersey Journal, aimed at Sylvia Miles: “last week the madcap mummer attended half a dozen openings, including one envelope, two appendectomies and a cellar door.”

June 1975 — the puppeteer Wayland Flowers reduces it to the portable form, in Earl Wilson’s syndicated column, collected by Barry Popik ↗: “Of gadabout Sylvia Miles: ‘She’d go to the opening of an envelope.’” By that October Wilson reported Miles had begun to like it.

18 August 1977 — Warhol takes the joke over in the first person in Melvin Maddocks’s Monitor column: “We go to openings of envelopes, openings of books — which are better — and closings of doors” (citation and full passage ↗).

23 February 1987 — the day after Warhol’s death, Newsday recalls him still playing with it: “Everyone says I’d go to the opening of an envelope. Well, last night I went to the opening of an escalator at Bergdorf’s. That’s almost as good as an envelope” (via Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: Maddocks introduced the passage as “the reasonably wise and certainly desperate words of a premier party-goer, Andy Warhol.” Transcribed from the Monitor column by Quote Investigator ↗, which verified it via ProQuest; the 1977 Monitor is not freely readable online.

author.name: Andy Warhol
author.heading: Who Andy Warhol was
author.metaLine: 1928–1987 · American pop artist, filmmaker & co-founder of Interview magazine
author.bio: Warhol turned soup cans, silkscreened Marilyns and disaster photographs into the defining images of American Pop art, then treated publicity itself as a medium — the Factory, the films, and Interview magazine, which he co-founded with John Wilcock in the autumn of 1969. Born in Pittsburgh on 6 August 1928, he was by the mid-1970s a fixture of the New York party circuit; Maddocks introduced him in the 1977 column as “a premier party-goer.” He died on 22 February 1987.

copyAttribution: “We go to openings of envelopes, openings of books — which are better — and closings of doors.” —Andy Warhol, quoted by Melvin Maddocks in “Cold showers and parties,” The Christian Science Monitor, 18 August 1977, p. 26. Warhol said the line, but did not coin the joke: the earliest documented version is Jack O’Brian’s barb at actress Sylvia Miles in The Jersey Journal, 23 January 1974.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Warhol genuinely spoke the words quoted above — and he is still the wrong answer to the question people usually mean, which is who coined the envelope joke. The two facts get collapsed constantly.

items.why: Mike Stanton’s Buddy Cianci biography The Prince of Providence (Random House, 2004; ©2003) has the mayor joking that he would attend the opening of an envelope “in a line borrowed from Andy Warhol” — one of many such credits collected by Barry Popik ↗. But the joke is in print from January 1974, more than three years before Warhol’s documented use of it, and it was not aimed at him.

The line most often pinned on Warhol is the third-person taunt — “She’d go to the opening of an envelope” — which Quote Investigator traces ↗ to the puppeteer Wayland Flowers, about Sylvia Miles, in Earl Wilson’s column in June 1975. Warhol’s own documented version is first-person and longer: “We go to openings of envelopes, openings of books — which are better — and closings of doors.”

items.who: Olivia Goldsmith, Buddy Cianci and others
items.why: The gag kept being re-pointed at whoever was currently over-exposed. Michelle Lovric’s Women’s Wicked Wisdom (2004) gives Olivia Goldsmith on Ivana Trump — “she shows up to the opening of an envelope” — and Quote Investigator records ↗ earlier variants swapping in Bob Hope, Cesar Romero and Michael York.

misattribution.truthLine: Warhol did say “We go to openings of envelopes” — in The Christian Science Monitor of 18 August 1977. He was riffing on a joke that, on the earliest evidence located by Quote Investigator ↗, Jack O’Brian had aimed at Sylvia Miles in January 1974 and Wayland Flowers had made famous by 1975.

context.heading: Why the joke stuck to him
lead: It was never about Warhol first. In January 1974 the Broadway columnist Jack O’Brian aimed an early, baroque version at the actress Sylvia Miles — who had starred in Warhol’s own film Heat (1972) — writing that she had lately attended “half a dozen openings, including one envelope, two appendectomies and a cellar door.” The puppeteer Wayland Flowers sanded it down to the version everyone remembers, and by the summer of 1975 Earl Wilson was running it in syndication: “She’d go to the opening of an envelope.”

Warhol’s move, in August 1977, was to take a joke about a compulsive party-goer and say it in the first person — and then keep going, past envelopes to book launches and the closing of doors. He never dropped it. In the Newsday piece that ran the day after his death, he is remembered saying he had just been to the opening of an escalator at Bergdorf’s, which was “almost as good as an envelope.”
context.detailsSummary: What happened to the line afterwards
detailsBody: The joke outlived everyone in it. By 2004 it had been recycled for a new set of names — Michelle Lovric’s Women’s Wicked Wisdom gives Olivia Goldsmith on Ivana Trump: “she shows up to the opening of an envelope” — and it became a standard weapon against publicity-hungry politicians, most famously the Providence mayor Buddy Cianci.

It has since stopped being a quotation at all. Wiktionary now lists ↗ “opening of an envelope” as a plain English idiom: any event that might contribute to one’s self-promotion. That drift is exactly why the coinage keeps getting handed to the most famous name in the story.
context.pull: “Everyone says I’d go to the opening of an envelope. Well, last night I went to the opening of an escalator at Bergdorf’s.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located version of the joke is Jack O'Brian's Broadway column in The Jersey Journal, 23 January 1974, aimed at Sylvia Miles: 'last week the madcap mummer attended half a dozen openings, including one envelope, two appendectomies and a cellar door.'

Andy Warhol was quoted saying 'We go to openings of envelopes, openings of books — which are better — and closings of doors' by columnist Melvin Maddocks in 'Cold showers and parties,' The Christian Science Monitor, 18 August 1977, quote page 26, column 3, introduced as 'the reasonably wise and certainly desperate words of a premier party-goer, Andy Warhol.'

Newsday, 23 February 1987 ('Hangin' Out With Andy' by Susan Mulcahy), quotes Warhol: 'Everyone says I'd go to the opening of an envelope. Well, last night I went to the opening of an escalator at Bergdorf's. That's almost as good as an envelope.'

QI's conclusion is that the barb was initially crafted by Jack O'Brian with Sylvia Miles as first target, that Wayland Flowers helped popularize it by 1975, and that Warhol employed the gag in a self-aware manner in 1977; QI also records the 2004 Michelle Lovric book giving Olivia Goldsmith on Ivana Trump, and 1994 variants naming Bob Hope, Cesar Romero and Michael York.
Earl Wilson's column (Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, 19 June 1975) reports Wayland Flowers on 'gadabout Sylvia Miles': 'She'd go to the opening of an envelope.'
Mike Stanton's 'The Prince of Providence' (Random House, 2004, ©2003) says Buddy Cianci joked that he would attend the opening of an envelope 'in a line borrowed from Andy Warhol'.
Wikiquote maintains a page of Andy Warhol quotations spanning the 1960s to 1980s.

Sylvia Miles (September 9, 1924 – June 12, 2019) starred in Andy Warhol's underground feature film 'Heat' (1972), and the article credits Wayland Flowers and his puppet Madame with first uttering the widely quoted 'opening of an envelope' line.
Wiktionary defines 'opening of an envelope' as an idiomatic, humorous noun phrase meaning any kind of event or activity that may contribute to one's self-promotion.
Melvin Maddocks wrote for The Christian Science Monitor in various roles, including arts editor and book review editor, from 1946 to 1989.
Andy Warhol was born August 6, 1928 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania and died February 22, 1987; he co-founded Interview magazine with John Wilcock in the fall of 1969.
